title: Autumn, at Ruby’s pace.
summary: James, Ruby, and the simple joys of autumn—with a sensory nature guide for sitting, walking, or rolling, and outings across all six New England states.
search: The journal / Simple joys Autumn in New England · From the family album Autumn, at Ruby’s pace. James, a very busy yellow Lab, and the pleasure of an ordinary autumn visit with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve. October 14, 2026 · Family story & practical nature guide A little walk together ↓Plan your own time outside ↓ James and Ruby, with autumn underfoot. From our family camera roll. James has the leash and a big grin. Ruby has her nose in the grass and apparently quite a lot to investigate. There are leaves scattered along the road, yellow beginning to show in the trees, and still enough warmth for shorts. A very New England sort of autumn. I love this photograph. James is looking up at the camera while Ruby gets on with the important business of being a dog. The leash makes a long white line between them. Around them, the season is quietly changing. A visit with Mom-Mom & Grandpa Steve (aka Grandma & Grandpa), a little time outside, and Ruby to walk. James is right in the middle of it all. It’s a simple way to spend the afternoon together. Autumn in New England gives us so much to look at on an everyday walk. Green leaves hang on beside the gold ones. A few have already landed at the edge of the pavement. I like this part of the season, when summer is still showing up in somebody’s outfit and the trees have begun moving on. And then there is Ruby, who seems perfectly prepared to spend the afternoon examining one small patch of grass. She makes a good case for taking our time. There may be something very interesting by the next leaf. There is so much texture in this picture: the rough edge of the road, the soft-looking grass, Ruby’s pale coat against the dark pavement. It makes me think about how many ways there are to meet a season. Looking is one. Listening, feeling the air, or simply spending a few minutes in a familiar place are others. Nobody needs to notice the same thing. What I want for James is room to be part of the day in his own way. A good afternoon doesn’t need a mileage goal, a completed activity, or a photograph in which everybody faces the camera. It can have pauses. It can change direction. It can end while there is still something left to see. These are the family photographs I keep coming back to: James smiling, Ruby nearby, and time with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve. A walk together belongs in the family album just as much as a holiday or a birthday. A dog, some leaves, and time with the grandparents. The simple joys of autumn, right here. If you’re planning some time outside this autumn, here are some ways to begin. A bench, a smooth path, a garden, a window overlooking a tree: there is more than one good way outside. The practical field guide · New EnglandA little nature, your way.A sensory walk can be a sit, a roll, or a few minutes at the doorstep. Choose what feels interesting and comfortable today; every suggestion is optional. Choose your paceExplore the sensesFind a placeBefore you go 01 · Make room for everyoneChoose the outing that fits today. Universal design starts with choices built into the plan: a usable route, somewhere to rest, information in more than one form, and an easy way to finish. These ideas are for children, teens, and adults, with and without disabilities. Choose by preferences and support needs, not an ability ranking. Stay in one lovely spotTry five minutes beside a tree, at a garden table, or on an accessible viewing deck. A seated companion can share the same view. On a home day, watch branches from a window or enjoy a familiar nature photograph together. Go a little way & returnPick a firm route with a known turnaround: the first bench or one tree. Check the distance both ways. Walking, using a wheelchair or walker, and bringing a stroller are all ways to enjoy the same small outing. Leave room to exploreIf everyone wants more, add another section after checking its surface and slope. Keep the shorter plan available. More distance is an option, never the measure of a good day. A choice counts without spoken words.Offer two real options—“tree or water?”—using speech, familiar photos, objects, sign, or the person’s usual AAC. Keep “stop,” “more,” “quiet,” “help,” “toilet,” and “home” available. Give time to respond; if pointing is difficult, offer choices one at a time using their established yes/no signal. Honor refusal and changes of mind.For a blind or low-vision companion, offer brief descriptions and ask before guiding. For a deaf or hard-of-hearing companion, keep the plan visible, face them when communicating, and agree on a visual signal for stopping. Ask before touching anyone or moving their mobility equipment. 02 · An invitation, never a checklistEight ways to meet the season.Start with one appealing idea. Keep it, change it, or skip it. A quiet setting for one person may feel busy to another; there is no need to use every sense or turn the afternoon into a lesson. 01 SightNotice one gold leaf, a cloud, or a reflection from a comfortable position. Bring a leaf into view only where handling is permitted; a companion can describe its shape and color.Make it gentler: Try shade, a brimmed hat, or a still view instead of sparkling water. Looking away is fine. 02 SoundPause for wind in the trees, a bird, or leaves underfoot. If listening is not useful or enjoyable, watch branches sway or notice a bird’s movement instead.Make it gentler: Use preferred hearing protection and move away from roads, leaf blowers, barking, or crowds. No “quiet listening” performance required. 03 TouchOffer a permitted tactile exhibit or a familiar leaf from home on a tray within comfortable reach. Touch with a fingertip, through a glove, or not at all. Do not place objects in someone’s hand without agreement.Make it gentler: A favorite fabric or fidget can come along. Leave unfamiliar plants, fungi, and wildlife untouched. 04 SmellNotice the air near a pine grove, a garden, or the shore from the path. Let the person choose the distance; there is no need to pick, crush, or bring plants close to a face.Make it gentler: Skip scent activities around allergies, nausea, or aversion. Move away from strong smells; bring no added fragrance. 05 TasteHave a familiar snack or drink at a comfortable stopping place. An autumn picnic can mean the food someone already enjoys; trying a new flavor is entirely optional.Make it work: Follow the person’s usual eating and drinking supports. A non-food pause is equally welcome. Do not taste wild berries, mushrooms, leaves, or water. 06 Movement & balance (vestibular sense)Choose a short, smooth stretch at the person’s preferred speed, or stay still and watch the scenery. A turn or change in pace should be expected and agreed on.Make it gentler: Avoid surprise pushing, spinning, steep slopes, and uneven shortcuts. A stable seated position is a full way to participate. 07 Body position & effort (proprioception)Notice comfortable contact with a seat, backrest, or foot support. If already comfortable and chosen, carrying a light water bottle or moving along the path can offer another way to notice effort.Make it gentler: No added weights, forced stretches, or endurance goals. Rest and familiar positioning supports belong on the outing. 08 Inside-body cues (interoception)Offer a concrete choice: “drink or rest?” “jacket on or off?” Check comfort, temperature, energy, and toilet needs without requiring anyone to name a body sensation.Make it easier: Offer planned breaks and usual supports even without a request. Pause or leave when discomfort appears. 03 · Six states, a few good starting pointsWhere might you begin?These are researched planning ideas, not reports that our family has visited every location or audited access. Official information was checked October 14, 2026. Follow the links for current conditions, fees, and facilities; an “accessible” trail label does not describe every person’s experience. MassachusettsDrumlin Farm · LincolnA small start: The 350-foot Ice Pond Trail offers a woodland-and-pond outing, with a guide rope, Braille stops, and an audio tour. The surface is crushed stone and the path is five feet wide.Check the fit: Mass Audubon notes that portions can still feel steep or strenuous. Accessible restrooms and equipment loans are listed; confirm availability. The farmyard adds animal sounds, smells, and visitors.With a dog? Pet dogs are not permitted; service animals are welcome.Drumlin Farm access details & photo tour · Visitor rules New HampshireOdiorne Point State Park · RyeA small start: Ask staff about an accessible approach to a seaside picnic spot, or a short section of the paved recreation path along Route 1A. Try watching waves or noticing the sea air.Check the fit: The roadside route may bring traffic noise; natural-surface trails are different terrain. The park currently flags dune-restoration trail closures. Confirm the exact route, gate access, and seasonal restroom opening before setting out.With a dog? Pet dogs are not permitted.NH Parks trail access information · Odiorne conditions, map & visitor rules MaineWolfe’s Neck Woods · FreeportA small start: The White Pines Trail is identified as accessible in Maine’s park access guide. Begin at the second parking lot and choose a short out-and-back among the pines toward the bay views.Check the fit: Other park trails include uneven ground and steps. The rocky shore is a separate access question. Confirm the current White Pines surface, restroom availability, and seasonal conditions.With a dog? Park guidance allows leashed, attended pets under control; check current rules before bringing yours.Wolfe’s Neck Woods visitor information & map · Maine park access guide (PDF) VermontNorth Branch Nature Center · MontpelierA small start: A 0.3-mile Universal Access Trail loops around meadows and the community garden. The center lists compacted crushed stone, three benches, and a typical width of five feet, narrowing to three feet.Check the fit: The published maximum grade and cross-slope are each 6%; winter surfaces vary. Ask about toilet access when the center is closed. Try a bench stop to watch grasses move.With a dog? The center’s policy requires pets to be leashed; only service animals are permitted indoors.North Branch trail measurements & map · Center animal policy Rhode IslandClaire D. McIntosh Wildlife Refuge · BristolA small start: Audubon describes an accessible crushed-stone trail and wooden boardwalk through marsh habitat toward Narragansett Bay, with less than a mile of trails overall. Enjoy grasses, birds, or a short boardwalk section.Check the fit: Confirm boardwalk conditions and the distance from parking to your chosen stopping point. Bathrooms are available during nature-center hours; do not rely on access outside those hours. Coastal wind and wet boards may change the experience.With a dog? Pet dogs are prohibited.McIntosh Refuge access details & rules ConnecticutHammonasset Beach State Park · MadisonA small start: Choose a short section of the park’s paved-and-boardwalk coastal route. The full listed walk is 3.4 miles; there is no reason to complete it to enjoy the view.Check the fit: This is a popular shared route. Ask about quieter times, the nearest accessible parking and open restroom, and sand on the path. The summer beach-access mat is seasonal, so do not assume an autumn route onto the sand.With a dog? Leashed pets are allowed in picnic areas year-round; beach access has seasonal dates. Check the rules for the exact area you plan to use.Hammonasset routes & pet rules · Seasonal beach access information Pet rules and service-animal access are different. If you need a specific accommodation, ask the site directly. For an outing without a drive or admission fee, begin with a familiar sidewalk, public garden, or tree near home after checking its route and seating. 04 · A small plan to take alongBefore you go.Pick the details that matter to your group. A few minutes of preparation can leave more room for simply being there. Check the whole route. Parking or drop-off, surface, slope, width, steps, gates, seating, and the return journey—not just the trail name. Ask about wheelchair space beside benches and usable picnic-table clearance. Check the practical essentials. Open accessible toilets, any needed changing facilities, fees, pet rules, and current closures. In autumn, ask about wet leaves, mud, early closing, and hunting-season restrictions where relevant. Show what will happen. Use the person’s preferred format: a photo, spoken explanation, large-print note, or short visual plan. For example: “Arrive → choose a spot → pause → return.” Make the turnaround clear. Pack familiar supports. AAC and backup communication, water, usual food or feeding supplies, layers, preferred hearing protection, and the personal care or mobility equipment you already use. Keep essentials within reach. Agree on help and a way out. Ask what assistance is wanted. Plan for roads, water edges, and anyone who may need close support. Choose a nearby rest point and an easy return before anyone is tired. Let the day be enough. Offer breaks and “all done” throughout. No required touching, tasting, speaking, eye contact, posing, or finishing the trail. Watch, listen, rest, or head home together. One tree. One patch of sky. One very interesting smell, if you happen to be Ruby. There is plenty to begin with. More from the family albumA few more good days. title: A littleEaster color.
summary: An Easter family visit to Berlin Farms in Massachusetts: colorful eggs, an enthusiastic bunny, wide-open fields and a few practical notes before you go.

A spring visit to Berlin FarmsA littleEaster color.An egg hunt, a bunny with a few good poses, and a family photograph worth keeping.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026From an earlier Easter visitPastel eggs across the lawn. White fences beyond the buildings. One orange jacket that had apparently declined the pastel dress code.Our Easter photographs from Berlin Farms deserved a little space in the journal. The family storyMap & visit detailsAccess & sensory notesMore photographs Opened from the family albumThe eggs were everywhere.There is a particular sort of New England spring photograph: green beginning to return to the grass, bare trees in the distance, and everybody sensibly still wearing a jacket. Our Berlin Farms pictures have all of that, with the addition of a lawn covered in pink, yellow, blue and green eggs.A canvas shopping bag is ready for the egg hunt. The Easter Bunny has a pink bow, a floral backdrop, and considerably more enthusiasm for posing than most adults can sustain. I especially like the photograph with the arms up. There is plenty happening in it, and that smile is the part I keep coming back to.Then there is the family picture: the three of us together, the bunny at one end, and the stone patio beneath our feet. I am glad we have that one. A canvas tote, a lawn full of eggs, and a very visible orange jacket.All of us in the frame. The bunny makes four. A little spring color. Original editorial illustration.Between the photographsA little room to look around.The farm makes a lovely setting for this chapter. White clapboard buildings sit beside lines of white fencing, with fields stretching beyond them. In one photograph, a horse is grazing in the distance. The colors are mostly green, white and gray, which leaves the orange jacket with very little competition.I like having a wider view among the close-ups. It brings back the shape of a place: the deck, the fence, the buildings around the egg-hunt lawn. A family album needs a little of the scenery, too. White fences, open fields, and a sky still considering its spring options. One for the albumThe good partis right here.The photographs beside the black door are worth keeping in the set. There is a cap being adjusted, a yellow egg on the grass, and four very large letters spelling LOVE. The farm has helpfully supplied the caption.A tote bag, a bunny, and a few photographs I am glad we took.That is what I want to keep from this Easter visit: the color on the lawn, the bunny pictures, and our family together in the middle of it.One more photograph beside the LOVE door. Practical careAccessible restrooms, changing equipment when published, parking, drop-off, seating, weather exposure and what remains unconfirmed. We prioritize current official venue information and use public visitor reports as a secondary reality check when helpful. Review anecdotes are labeled as such; they never overwrite current organizer facts. Read the complete instructions.The details left inThe useful part, in full.Open just what you need.Put today’s plan first.+A useful handover helps the next person act. Begin with today’s date, the agreed time together, what the person is expecting and anything that has changed. Keep the long history in its appropriate record. Make the plan with the person receiving support, using the communication they prefer and any assistance they need. Explain who is arriving, what is happening and how the visit will finish. Offer choices within the arrangements that are genuinely available. Before responsibility changes hands Confirm the incoming person has arrived and has agreed to take over.Review the important changes and invite questions.Check they can access the needed supplies, contacts and current instructions.Confirm what happens if plans change or the return is delayed. When support needs uninterrupted coverage, do not rely on an unanswered message as a completed handoff. Show how communication works today.+Have the person’s usual communication tools available and ready to use, including a familiar backup if they have one. Show the incoming supporter where they are kept and explain any practical help needed to use them. Do not replace a familiar system with a new worksheet simply because the worksheet is convenient. Share the useful basics: how the person makes a choice, asks for help, signals a pause and indicates that they want to finish. If a signal is uncertain, say so. “This sometimes means a break; check with them” is more useful than presenting a guess as a fixed fact. The NJC Communication Bill of Rights supports meaningful choices, direct communication and access to working communication systems. The practical goal here is that the person can still participate when their usual supporter is away. Keep current care instructions alongside the short note.+The handover is a summary of arrangements, not a substitute for the person’s current care, medical or emergency plans. Confirm that the incoming supporter is authorized, trained where necessary and able to provide the support being transferred. Give them access to the actual instructions and essential information they need, through the established private channel. Do not omit a critical safety detail merely to keep the summary to one page. Equally, do not improvise medication directions, eating or drinking instructions, lifting methods or emergency procedures in this template. If instructions conflict, are out of date or cannot be accessed, resolve the issue with the appropriate person before the affected activity or handoff. Follow the existing emergency arrangements for urgent situations. The short handover template.+Use these headings in the private record or on the paper system you already use. The blank version is deliberately general. Add only the information appropriate for this recipient and setting; keep completed copies secure. Date and timePrepared: ______ · Support begins: ______ · Expected finish: ______ Today’s agreed planFirst: ______ · Then: ______ · The shorter version: ______ The person’s choicesWhat they have chosen: ______ · What is still open: ______ CommunicationTools and location: ______ · Useful partner guidance: ______ · Backup: ______ Food, drink and ordinary suppliesWhat is ready: ______ · Where the relevant current instructions are kept: ______ A pause or finishHow to check: ______ · Available place or option: ______ Changes that matter todayConfirmed changes: ______ · Question to resolve before handoff: ______ Current care and emergency instructionsPrivate location and version/date: ______ · Access checked: ______ Contacts and changes of planAgreed contact route: ______ · Backup route: ______ · Return-delay plan: ______ Responsibility acceptedOutgoing supporter: ______ · Incoming supporter: ______ · Time confirmed: ______ A completed handover can contain private information. Do not put it on a public noticeboard, leave it in a shared vehicle or paste it into an open online tool. Use the person’s agreed permissions and the provider’s requirements for storage and sharing. What a useful note sounds like.+Illustrative example: “Today we agreed on the library and home. The shorter version is returning the books only. The communication bag is beside the coat and has been checked. Please confirm the current return time with me before I leave.” This example does not contain the safety instructions for a real person. Those still need to be accessible to the person providing support. Close the handover at the other end.+Before leaving, give a brief factual update: what took place, what changed, anything needing attention and who has agreed to the next step. Complete required records in the proper system. Confirm that the next supporter has accepted responsibility where continuous support is needed. Revise the standing information when something changes. Remove an outdated copy so it cannot be mistaken for the current plan.
